summary: Five-lens visual review of a built V15 chapter, with skeptic verification of serious findings

confirmed.description: The Fisherman's age and hair change from panel to panel. The script's man in his forties has black curly hair and a grizzled beard on page 2, in 4.1, 4.2, 5.1 to 5.5, 6.3 and 6.5. In 3.1, 3.4, 3.5, 4.4, 4.5, 6.1 and 6.2 he is a visibly older man, fifties to sixties, with heavily grey hair and a lined face. In 6.1 he is also slight and narrow-faced instead of stocky. He does not read as one person across the chapter.
confirmed.evidence: 3.5 crop: hair mostly grey, deeply lined face, grey beard. 2.2 and 4.2 crops: black hair, younger face. 6.1: a thin grey-haired man sits between the Woman and Nagoji, with no stocky build and no red lungi visible. Script 2.1: 'forties ... short grizzled beard ... hold them for the chapter'.

verdict.reason: The drift is real, but it is minor, not major. I put 19 Fisherman crops side by side. His hair is black and curly in 2.1, 2.2, 2.4, 4.1, 4.2, 5.1 to 5.5, 6.3 and 6.5. It is clearly salt-and-pepper in 3.1, 3.4, 3.5, 4.4, 4.5, 6.1 and 6.2, and his face looks more lined and older there. The change is visible at print size, most of all in 3.4 and 3.5, then back to black hair in 4.2 and grey again in 4.4 on the same page. Script 2.1 says to establish the faces and 'hold them for the chapter', so this is a continuity miss. Still, he always reads as the same man. He keeps the same broad face, the same grizzled grey beard and moustache, and the same costume in every panel: cream vest, white cloth on the left shoulder, and the red lungi wherever it is in frame (6.2, for example). He is the only speaker with a shoulder cloth, and he can't be mistaken for the Wary Fisherman, who is gaunt, has a long beard and wears a brown vest with a net. The script fixes only a 'grizzled' beard and an age in his forties, not black hair, and greying hair fits that age. In 6.1 he looks slighter because he is a small mid-ground figure behind two balloons. Tonal wobble with no identity confusion is polish, not a localized clear error. The fix is to darken the hair in 3.1, 3.4, 3.5, 4.4, 4.5, 6.1 and 6.2 (or unify it the other way) when those frames are next touched.

confirmed.description: The Wary Fisherman is off-model. Established in 2.1, 2.4 and 3.4 as an older gaunt man with a long grey-streaked beard and grey hair, here he has thick black curly hair, a short dark goatee-style beard and a fuller, younger face. Only the net and costume identify him.
confirmed.evidence: Zoomed crop of 3.3: black curly hair, short beard darker than grey, not gaunt. Compare 3.4 (left figure): long grey beard, grey hair, gaunt. Script 2.1: 'older and gaunt, long grey-streaked beard'.

verdict.reason: Confirmed. I zoomed in on page 3, panel 3 (the lone figure ankle-deep in the surf, net on his shoulder, speaking both angle-bracket balloons). He has thick black curly hair, a short trimmed beard that is mostly dark with some grey at the chin, and a fuller, younger face. Everywhere else in the chapter the Wary Fisherman is the older, gaunt man with grey stringy hair and a long grey beard: 2.1 (right face), 2.4, 3.4 (left figure, directly below this panel), 4.1 and 4.5. Script 2.1 says 'older and gaunt, long grey-streaked beard' and 'Establish the three faces now and hold them for the chapter'. The 3.3 description does not relax this. CONTINUITY.md has no entry for him. The head is small (about 85 px, roughly 7 mm at print). Even so, black versus grey hair and a short versus long beard show at normal page view, especially with 3.4 stacked right under it. In 3.3 he looks closer to the leader Fisherman's model (short grizzled beard, black curly hair). One nuance on the report: the beard is not entirely dark, it has some grey at the chin, but it is short and nowhere near the long grey beard he has elsewhere. It is not a blocker because his costume (dark brown vest, off-white lungi, coiled net), the balloon tails and his position alone at the tide line still identify him. So he is off-model but not misidentified: a localized fix, redraw the head only.

confirmed.description: The brand is missing from the panel that is built around it. Nagoji's left forearm is not turned toward camera and no brand is visible anywhere, so the Woman's gaze has nothing to land on. She looks down at his face or chest instead. The bible's chapter 4 row requires the brand to be visible, and the script requires it here.
confirmed.evidence: 5.4 crop: Nagoji lies back between the Fisherman and the Woman, and only his head, shoulder and upper chest are in frame. No forearm is shown. Script 5.4: 'LEFT forearm turned toward camera across his body so the brand on its inner side shows ... her gaze fixed on the brand'.

verdict.reason:
Confirmed on page 5, panel 4. In the crop, Nagoji lies back between the Fisherman (left, mid-gesture) and the Young Fisherman (right). Only his head, shoulder and a strip of upper chest and torn tunic are in frame. Neither forearm appears anywhere in the panel, so no brand is drawn. The Woman looks down toward his face and chest, so her gaze has nothing to land on. Script 5.4 asks for exactly the opposite: "LEFT forearm turned toward camera across his body so the brand on its inner side shows ... her gaze fixed on the brand". Nothing in the script's notes allows leaving it out.

The reviewer overstates one point. The bible's chapter 4 row says the brand is visible "for the first time" in this chapter, and that is already met by the 3.2 close-up of the brand. The bible does not require the brand in this particular panel; the script does.

The miss is compounded on the same page. In 5.3 the line "Look at his mark" is spoken while no mark is visible, and in 5.5 the brand the script calls for is also out of frame. As a result, page 5 never shows the brand that drives the Woman's decision to "send word to the kapitan".

The dialogue still carries the plot, so this is not a lost beat or a blocker. It is still a clear, localized staging error against the script, in the one panel built around the brand, and it is plainly visible at print size. Severity: major.

confirmed.description: The brand and hands that the kapitan appraises are out of frame. Nagoji is cropped at the shoulders in the lower left corner, so the 'weighing' beat has no object and the brand does not show in the chapter's closing image.
confirmed.evidence: 6.5: Nagoji appears only as head and shoulders at the bottom left edge. There is no left forearm on the mat. Script 6.5: 'Nagoji's left forearm lies on the mat, inner side up, toward him'.

verdict.reason: Confirmed on page 6, panel 5 (I zoomed into a crop of the bottom tier). The panel shows Nagoji only as a head and bare shoulders in the lower left. The panel's bottom border cuts him off at the collarbone. There is no forearm, no hand and no mat surface in frame, so the brand cannot be seen. Script 6.5 asks for this directly: "Nagoji's left forearm lies on the mat, inner side up, toward him", and the kapitan's look should move "over the brand, the hands, the shoulders". The notes also make the left inner forearm the brand's placement for the chapter. Nothing in the bible or script allows leaving it out, and at print size it is plainly absent, not just too small to see. One correction to the report: the weighing still has an object. The kapitan's downward gaze is aimed at Nagoji's face, and the three captions ("horse trader's eyes", "market squares", "I was being weighed") carry the beat, so a reader still follows it. What is lost is the brand, which the script wanted as the thing being appraised in the closing image. That makes this a crop and staging error confined to one panel, not a missing story beat. Severity: major, not blocker.

confirmed.description: Wrong speaker tails assign the Fisherman's lines to the wrong people. '<Half is still half.>' and 'You fought them, yes?' both point to Nagoji, so he seems to ask himself whether he fought them. '<What? He is half dead.>' is an off-panel line from the Wary Fisherman, but its tail points to the Fisherman's head.
confirmed.evidence: 3.5 crop: the two lower balloons' tails end at Nagoji's face and mouth, and the top balloon's tail ends at the Fisherman's hair. Script: the Wary Fisherman speaks off-panel, and the Fisherman says the other two lines.

verdict.reason: Confirmed on page 3, panel 5, after cropping it at full resolution. The tail of '<What? He is half dead.>' ends in the Fisherman's grey hair, so the Fisherman appears to say it. The script makes it an off-panel line from the Wary Fisherman, so the tail should run to the panel edge. '<Half is still half.>' has its tail ending at Nagoji's hairline and temple. 'You fought them, yes?' has its tail ending at Nagoji's cheek and mouth. The script gives both lines to the Fisherman. At print size this reads as a clear exchange that runs the wrong way: the Fisherman objects, and Nagoji argues for his own worth and asks himself whether he fought them. It also loses the script's key beat, where the Fisherman switches to Konkani (the one plain balloon) to speak to Nagoji directly. Neither the bible nor the script allows these tails. The brief lists a wrong speaker tail as major, and the fix is local: redraw the three tails, with the top one pointing off-panel and the two lower ones pointing to the Fisherman. The art does not need to be redrawn.

confirmed.description: Nagoji's line 'That is enough.' has a tail pointing to the Fisherman, which gives the Fisherman Nagoji's defiant closing line. The tail of 'You know the name.' ends in open sky between the two men and is ambiguous.
confirmed.evidence: 4.4 crop: the 'That is enough.' balloon sits over the Fisherman's chest, with its tail pointing right toward his face. Script: NAGOJI: 'That is enough.'

verdict.reason: Confirmed as major, though the reviewer described the mechanism slightly wrong. On page 4, panel 4, the "That is enough." balloon sits entirely over the Fisherman's chest and shoulder cloth. Its wedge tail does not point up at the Fisherman's face as the reviewer said. It runs straight right, level with Nagoji's mouth. But the tip stops on the outer edge of the Fisherman's upper arm, inside his outline, about 0.7 in short of Nagoji's face at print size (the panel is about 5 in wide). The balloon body and the tail tip are both on the Fisherman, so a reader will give him the line. That misreading also makes sense in context ("that is enough" as the Fisherman closing the haggle before 4.5), so the reader would not notice the swap. Nagoji loses the defiant closing line the script gives him (NAGOJI: 'That is enough.'). The reading order is also unclear. This balloon sits at the far left and overlaps the height of the "I know they have not yet learned to kneel..." balloon, so it may be read before Nagoji's longer line, not after it. The second part of the claim does not hold up. The "You know the name." tail ends in sky above Nagoji's head, but it aims down and left along a line that meets the Fisherman's mouth, and the context after "Travancore." in 4.3 makes the speaker clear. That part is minor at most. The fix is local re-lettering, not a redraw: move "That is enough." next to Nagoji, below or after his first balloon, with the tail tip reaching him. That fits major (wrong speaker tail), not blocker.

confirmed.description: The girl's '<Portuguese.>' balloon has its tail on the Young Fisherman. That makes him call Nagoji Portuguese, and in 5.3 he appears to contradict himself.
confirmed.evidence: 5.2 crop: the tail ends at the Young Fisherman's headband. The whispering girl is in the lower left foreground with no balloon. Script: GIRL: '<Portuguese.>'

verdict.reason: Confirmed from a zoomed crop of page 5, panel 2. The tail of the "<Portuguese.>" balloon comes out to the left and its point sits on the Young Fisherman's headband, right across his eyes. He is the man in the blue vest carrying Nagoji's legs, and the tail is clearly aimed at him. The script gives the line to the GIRL. She is in the lower-left foreground with her hand at her mouth, whispering to the child next to her, and she has no balloon or tail of her own. Read as lettered, the Young Fisherman calls Nagoji Portuguese in 5.2, then in 5.3 turns and says "<No. Look at his eyes. Look at his mark.> <This one is enemy of the Portuguese.>" That reads as him contradicting himself, and it loses the beat where he rebukes the girl. The tail is large, so this will show at print size. The fix is only in the lettering: move the balloon to the left side of the panel and point its tail at the girl, or use a small whisper balloon with a dashed outline. The tail should also stop covering the Young Fisherman's eyes. This is a wrong speaker tail, which the rubric rates as major, not a blocker, because the art does not need to be redrawn.

confirmed.description: The Woman's first line '<Bring him in.>' has its tail on the thatch over the Fisherman's head, so it reads as his line.
confirmed.evidence: 5.4 crop: the balloon is at the top left, with its tail angled to the roof edge directly above the Fisherman. The Woman stands centre right. Script: WOMAN: '<Bring him in.>'

verdict.reason: I confirmed this on a full-resolution crop of page 5, panel 4. The '<Bring him in.>' balloon is in the top-left corner. Its tail ends at the left edge of the thatch, about 25 px (under 0.1 in at 300 DPI) above and to the right of the Fisherman's hair. The Woman's head is about 300 px (roughly 1 in) further right, so the nearest head to the tail tip is the Fisherman's. The Fisherman is drawn with his mouth open and one hand out in a talking gesture, as the script asks ('mid-gesture, talking'). That makes him the obvious speaker for a tail that stops over his head. The Woman's mouth is closed and her eyes are down. Her second balloon's tail points clearly at her. Read left to right, the panel comes out as the Fisherman saying 'Bring him in.' and the Woman answering with conditions. That makes sense as a reading, so nobody will stop to question it. But it takes the decision away from her, and the page intro calls her 'the woman who decides'. The tail's angle does point roughly toward her, but it stops well short of her, right above the Fisherman. Neither the script nor the bible allows this, and at print size the tail is clearly visible, so it is not too slight to matter. It is a wrong speaker tail on a single balloon: the art needs no change, only a longer tail or a re-placed balloon that reaches the Woman. So major, not blocker.

confirmed.description: 'She asks what they did to you.' has its tail on Nagoji, so he appears to ask the question and then answer it himself in 'Asked questions.'
confirmed.evidence: 5.5 crop: both balloons' tails converge on Nagoji's face and shoulder. The Fisherman at the left has none. Script: FISHERMAN: 'She asks what they did to you.'

verdict.reason: I confirmed this on a zoomed crop of page 5, panel 5. The tail of "She asks what they did to you." ends on Nagoji's face, on his cheek just below his eye. The tail of "Asked questions." ends on Nagoji's shoulder. The Fisherman is drawn at the left of the panel with no balloon pointing at him, yet the script gives the first line to him (FISHERMAN: "She asks what they did to you.") and only the reply to Nagoji. As lettered, Nagoji seems to translate the question to himself and then answer it. Context lets a reader work it out, since "to you" makes no sense from Nagoji, but the tail clearly points at the wrong person and is easy to see at print size. The fix is local: re-letter the first tail so it points at the Fisherman on the left. The art does not need redrawing. By the brief's severity scale, a wrong speaker tail is major.

confirmed.description: All three balloon tails in 3.5 point at the wrong speaker. '<What? He is half dead.>' is the Wary Fisherman's line, spoken off panel, but its tail lands on the Fisherman's head. '<Half is still half.>' and 'You fought them, yes?' are both the Fisherman's lines, but their tails point at Nagoji's face. As lettered, Nagoji asks himself whether he fought the Portuguese, and the chapter's first Konkani line is lost.
confirmed.evidence: Page 3, bottom panel. The tail of the top balloon ends on the grey-haired Fisherman at left. The tails of the two right-hand balloons end at Nagoji's hair and moustache.

verdict.reason:
Confirmed from a zoomed crop of page 3, panel 5 (bottom panel of /Users/roshanvenugopal/Documents/github/nagoji/output/comic-v15-full-redo/chapters/ch04/renders/r1/page-03.png). Only two people are in the panel. On the left is the grey-haired, grey-bearded Fisherman in a white vest and shoulder cloth, the same man as the centre figure in 3.4. On the right is Nagoji, with a clean chin, a thick moustache and the ochre tunic. The Wary Fisherman is not drawn.

The script gives the lines as follows:
- "<What? He is half dead.>" is the Wary Fisherman, off panel.
- "<Half is still half.>" is the Fisherman.
- "You fought them, yes?" is the Fisherman, in Konkani.

The lettering does something different:
- The tail of "<What? He is half dead.>" ends on the Fisherman's grey hair.
- The tail of "<Half is still half.>" ends at Nagoji's temple and hairline.
- The tail of "You fought them, yes?" ends at Nagoji's moustache and cheek.

So all three tails are wrong, and they are clear at print size. The effect is worse than a stray tail. The haggle reads backwards: the Fisherman now objects that the man is half dead, and Nagoji argues for his own worth. Nagoji also appears to speak Malayalam, which contradicts the caption in 3.3 ("I could not follow a word"). Nagoji then seems to ask himself "You fought them, yes?", so the chapter's key beat is lost: the Fisherman switching to Konkani to speak to him directly. The script calls this beat out on the page 3 intro and in the language-convention note.

The fix is re-lettering, not new art. The off-panel balloon needs a tail to the panel edge or no tail, and both Fisherman balloons need tails pointing to the man at left. That probably means moving the two right-hand balloons, because tails from the right would have to cross Nagoji. I am keeping this at blocker rather than major because the lettering puts the wrong words in the wrong mouths and a scripted story beat is lost.

confirmed.description: The girl's whispered '<Portuguese.>' has its tail on the Young Fisherman's head. He appears to call Nagoji Portuguese, and in the very next panel he contradicts himself ('No. Look at his eyes'). The speaker is the girl in the left foreground.
confirmed.evidence: Page 5, panel 2. The balloon's tail ends at the Young Fisherman's headband (centre right). The girls whispering are at far left.

verdict.reason: I'm confirming this one, but as major, not blocker. On page 5, panel 2, I zoomed in on a crop at full resolution. The tail of the '<Portuguese.>' balloon runs left from the balloon and its point sits on the Young Fisherman's headband and forehead. He is the right-hand carrier in the blue vest, at the centre right of the panel. Script 5.2 gives the line to GIRL, the small girl in the left foreground. In the art she and another child are at the far left, and her hand is raised to her mouth in a whisper. Nothing in the script or the continuity bible lets the Young Fisherman say this line. As lettered, he calls Nagoji Portuguese and then in 5.3 says '<No. Look at his eyes...>', so he contradicts himself. The error shows clearly at print size. It is not blocker level because the task's own scale lists a wrong speaker tail as major. The art is correct, since the whispering girl is drawn exactly where the script puts her. The fix is lettering only: move the balloon, or reroute its tail down-left to the girl. Nothing needs to be redrawn.

confirmed.description: 'She asks what they did to you.' is the Fisherman's relay line, but its tail points into Nagoji's face. Nagoji seems to ask and answer his own question. 'Asked questions.' then points at his shoulder.
confirmed.evidence: Page 5, bottom panel. The upper balloon's tail ends between Nagoji's eye and moustache. The Fisherman is at left with no tail on him.

verdict.reason: Confirmed on page 5, panel 5 (bottom strip). In the zoomed crop, the tail of the upper balloon ("She asks what they did to you.") ends on Nagoji's cheek, between his eye and his moustache. The Fisherman is at far left and no tail points to him. The lower balloon ("Asked questions.") has its tail on Nagoji's right shoulder. Read together, both balloons belong to Nagoji, so he appears to ask the question and then answer it. Script 5.5 gives the first line to the FISHERMAN, so the tail really does name the wrong speaker. The art itself is right: the Fisherman squats at left, the Woman washes Nagoji at right, and the tunic is off with the dhoti on. The fix is only in the lettering: move the upper balloon to the left or redirect its tail to the Fisherman's mouth, and ideally move the lower tail from the shoulder to Nagoji's mouth. No redraw is needed. The brief lists a wrong speaker tail as major, and the "relay" wording gives the reader only a weak hint, so this is major, not blocker.

confirmed.description: The balloon reading order is scrambled. '<We might as well gain something.>' sits top-left, so it is read first. The script order is Dutch questions, then 'marata on the sand', then 'We might as well gain something.' The Fisherman's argument now opens with its conclusion.
confirmed.evidence: Page 3, panel 4. The top-left balloon reads 'We might as well gain something'. The top-right reads 'The Portuguese and the Dutch ask questions anyway'. The lower right reads 'You think leaving one marata...'.

verdict.reason: The problem is real. On page 3, panel 4, the two top balloons start at the same height. The left one, "<We might as well gain something.>", is therefore read first. After it comes the top-right balloon, "<The Portuguese and the Dutch ask questions anyway.>", and last the lower-right "marata on the sand" balloon. Lines 95-99 of the script give the reverse order: the Dutch questions, then the marata line, then "We might as well gain something." as the conclusion. Both top tails point at the Fisherman, so nothing on the page signals that the right balloon should be read first. His argument now opens with its conclusion and loses its build-up. "Might as well" also depends on a reason that has not been given yet. The text itself is correct and the speaker is right, so the fix is only to re-letter the balloons: swap the two top balloons, or move "gain something" to the lower-right slot and shift the others up. That makes it major, not a blocker.

confirmed.description: The balloon order is reversed, and the second tail is ambiguous. 'Come, bhau. Before the crabs claim you.' sits left, so it is read first. The script has 'You see, he has a tongue as well as scars.' first. The small tail of the 'You see' balloon points toward Nagoji's head rather than the grinning Fisherman. The carry also does not read: the Young Fisherman crouches in mid-frame with no hold on Nagoji's legs, which are hidden behind the balloons. The sand crab is missing.
confirmed.evidence: Page 4, bottom panel. The left balloon reads 'Come, bhau...' and the right balloon reads 'You see...'. That balloon's tail tip is at Nagoji's head. Nagoji's legs are covered by the balloons.

verdict.reason: Confirmed on page 4, panel 5 (bottom strip), after zooming at 2x. (1) The balloon order is reversed. The left balloon, "Come, bhau. Before the crabs claim you.", sits at about the same height as the right balloon, "You see, he has a tongue as well as scars." Left-to-right reading therefore puts "Come, bhau" first. The script (4.5) puts "You see..." first, as the Fisherman's reaction to Nagoji's "That is enough," and then the invitation. The swap spoils the joke. (2) The second balloon's tail is small. It runs behind the left balloon and comes out above it pointing up and to the left. Its tip sits just right of Nagoji's chin and shoulder, at about page x708, y2390, not at the Fisherman's grinning face (about x530, y2255). A reader could take the line as Nagoji's, which makes no sense ("he has a tongue"). (3) The carry reads only in part. The Fisherman does hold Nagoji's shoulders from behind. The Young Fisherman crouches in mid-frame looking left, and his hands and Nagoji's legs are hidden behind the two balloons, so the "takes his legs" beat is not visible. (4) There is no sand crab. The foreground is almost entirely covered by the balloons. Nothing in the script or the bible allows the reversed order. Severity is major, not blocker, because the text itself is correct and legible and the identities are right. The fix is local: re-letter by swapping the balloon positions and re-aiming the 'You see' tail at the Fisherman. The missing crab and the hidden leg-carry are minor extras within this finding.

confirmed.description: The weather breaks continuity within the page. Panel 3.1 has a bright blue sky with sunlit white cumulus. The very same scene in 3.3, 3.4 and 3.5, and all of page 2, is under a flat, grey storm sky. The 3.2 insert also has bright sunny bokeh.
confirmed.evidence: Page 3, panel 1. The sky behind the three figures is saturated blue with fluffy clouds. Panels 3.3 to 3.5 below it show heavy grey overcast and storm surf.

verdict.reason: Confirmed on the crop. On page 3, panel 1, the sky behind the three figures is a clear, saturated blue with bright white cumulus clouds, and the sea and palms are in full sun. The scene carries straight on in panels 3.3, 3.4 and 3.5 (same beach, same cast, same wreck), and there the sky is heavy grey overcast over storm surf. All of page 2 is the same grey storm sky, and the script sets it up that way: 1.1 says "flat grey sky" and 2.1 says "lowering grey sky". Nothing in the script or the continuity bible allows the weather to clear for 3.1. It then turns grey again one panel later, so the reader sees the weather flip back and forth inside one continuous exchange. That is easy to see at print size, because 3.1 is a full-width strip at the top of the page, directly above the grey 3.3. The warm, sunlit bokeh in the 3.2 insert adds to the problem, but it is a small, tight close-up, so on its own it would be minor. The fault is contained in one panel: repaint or regenerate the 3.1 background under the grey overcast sky and leave the figures as they are. That makes it major, not a blocker.

confirmed.description: The weather jumps inside one continuous conversation. Page 3 and the left half of 4.1 are storm-grey. Panels 4.2 to 4.5 are blazing sun with a clear blue sky, calm turquoise sea and dry, fluffy hair on Nagoji. This is the same unbroken exchange on the same beach, with no time cut.
confirmed.evidence: Page 4, panels 2, 3, 4 and 5 are all sunny blue sky. Panel 4.1 still has dark storm clouds, and page 3, panels 3 to 5, are grey overcast.

verdict.reason:
Confirmed on the renders. Page 2 is heavy storm-grey throughout. Page 3, panels 3 to 5, are grey and overcast, with dark cloud and churning white surf. Page 4, panel 1 (checked in a crop) is still mostly grey storm cloud with only patches of blue, crashing white surf round the wreck, and sunlit palms at the right edge. Page 4, panel 2 then jumps to a clear blue sky with white cumulus, strong sun, a turquoise sea and palms running into bright haze. Panels 4.3, 4.4 and 4.5 stay sunny with blue skies. In 4.3 Nagoji's hair looks mostly dry, although the script for 4.1 says water is still running from it.

This is one unbroken exchange on the same beach. 3.5 ends "You fought them, yes?" and 4.1 answers "Yes," so there is no time cut. 1.4 is the only place the script allows the light to shift, and page 2 is still grey after it. Nothing in the script or CONTINUITY.md asks the sky to clear before the walk inland on page 5. Page 5 can be sunny because it comes after a scene change.

It also matters at print size. Pages 28 and 29 face each other as a spread, so grey 3.3 to 3.5 and sunny 4.2 to 4.5 sit side by side. Page 3, panel 1 also has partial blue sky, so the weather wobbles across both pages.

It stays major, not blocker, because every beat, identity and line of lettering is right. The fix is local: regrade or regenerate 4.2 to 4.5 with the storm-spent overcast sky, perhaps just starting to break, so the clearing happens gradually and continues into page 5.

confirmed.description: The wreck's design is not held from panel to panel. In 2.4 it is a single high-sided hull with a carved stern castle, heeled on the reef. In 4.1 it becomes two or three open skeletal hull frames with several standing masts, right against the beach rocks. In 4.5 it has standing masts with tattered sails still set. The script's broken mainmast is not shown in any of these. Panel 4.1 also shrinks Nagoji to a disembodied head at the bottom edge, where the script asks for a wide reset with 'every figure at full scale' and him up on one elbow.
confirmed.evidence: Page 4, panel 1: skeletal wreck frames at left and centre, and Nagoji only visible from the nose up between the Fisherman and the Young Fisherman. Page 4, panel 5: a masted ship with hanging sails at right. Page 2, panel 4: a carved-stern hull.

verdict.reason: I confirmed this in zoomed crops. Page 2, panel 4 shows a single intact, high-sided galleon with a carved stern castle, heeled over on a reef offshore. Page 4, panel 1 swaps it for two open, skeletal rib-frame hulls with several standing masts. One is at the left and one at the centre, and both sit right against the beach rocks, not on a distant reef. Page 4, panel 4 shows another ribbed hulk at the right. Page 4, panel 5 shows a masted ship with tattered sails still set. Only minutes pass in the story, and a ship cannot go from an intact hull to bare ribs to a ship with sails set in that time. None of these panels clearly shows the snapped mainmast the script asks for. The script ties this wreck to the ship in chapters 2 and 3 and describes it offshore on a reef. The left wreck in panel 4.1 takes up about a third of the panel, so readers will notice the change at print size. The staging point is also correct. In panel 4.1 the script calls for a wide shot that resets the geography, with 'every figure at full scale' and Nagoji 'up on one elbow'. The reviewer's page numbers (26 to 31) are book folios, not a different problem. Whether to change the house style to show the title on openers only is a book-wide design choice, not a problem on this page, so the finding is refuted.
